definition: Substantiate means to support a claim with solid evidence.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word substantiate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know substantiate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A single receipt substantiated her version of the evening better than an hour of argument could.
Support is the milder word — any evidence that leans a claim's way supports it, while substantiate demands enough solid evidence to hold the claim up on its own.
Prove goes further than substantiate: a substantiated claim stands firmly supported, while a proven one is settled beyond argument.

To back a claim is to stand behind it — adding your name, your agreement, or your reputation to it, often informally. Substantiate deals in evidence instead of endorsement: a substantiated claim rests on documents and facts, while a backed one may still rest on somebody's word.

Bolster strengthens a claim that already has some footing — fresh evidence shoring up a case half-built. Substantiate does the whole job from nothing: it gives a bare claim the solid support it needs to stand at all. You bolster what stands shakily; you substantiate what has not yet stood.
to knock the support out from under a claim
to show the claim is false outright

The tribe's oral history put the fishing village at the river bend for six centuries, and the archaeologists' report substantiated it layer by layer: hearth charcoal dated to the 1400s, netting weights in every stratum, and pollen from the very crops the stories named.
Substantiate is exact because a claim — the oral history — is being given solid evidence to stand on; the word literally means giving a claim substance.
Authenticate would test whether an object is genuine; corroborate, which you met in this unit's readings, adds a second independent voice.
Substantiate is evidence shoring up the claim itself.
Substantiate lives in law, journalism, and grant offices: claims get substantiated with documents, figures, and dated records.
Corroborate — met in this unit's readings — is its cousin for confirmation by a second independent source.
And keep the split with authenticate: things are authenticated, claims are substantiated.

For ninety years, Milford's welcome sign has called its covered bridge the oldest in the state.
When a rival town challenged the boast last spring, the historical society realized no one had ever substantiated it.
The claim rested entirely on a 1930s pamphlet, which cited nothing but town pride.
So volunteers pulled county ledgers, timber invoices, and a surveyor's diary from 1841 -- documents that could hold the date up on their own.
The file they assembled settled the matter for good: the bridge kept its title, and the sign, for once, told a checkable truth.
